strengths: The paper identifies a real gap: existing LLM memory benchmarks focus on static long-context reading comprehension and lack evaluation of procedural memory/continual learning from user feedback; MemoryBench is a timely attempt to fill this gap (Sections 1, 2.1).

It assembles a broad set of 11 public datasets spanning open/legal/academic domains, English/Chinese, and four input-output formats (LiSo/SiLo/LiLo/SiSo), with a unified task representation (q, v, c) (Section 2.3, Table 2).

The framework is modular and clearly described: Task Provider, User Simulator, and Performance Monitor, with a taxonomy of declarative (semantic/episodic) vs procedural memory and explicit (verbose/action) vs implicit feedback (Sections 2.1-2.2, Figure 1).

The experiments are extensive: 8 baselines including RAG variants and recent memory systems, off-policy/on-policy settings, Qwen3-8B/32B backbones, and detailed time/memory analysis (Section 3, Tables 7-15, Figure 3).

The negative results are useful: recent memory systems often do not outperform simple RAG baselines and are inefficient, providing a cautionary benchmark for the community (Section 3.3, Tables 9 and 14).
The paper includes with/without feedback comparisons and states that simulated feedback logs and code are released, supporting reproducibility and future work (A.3.5, A.3.9, Section 7).
weaknesses: The validity of the simulated user feedback is not established. The simulator is given ground-truth/evaluation metadata, so its feedback can be oracle-like and may not reflect real user behavior; no human study or correlation with real user feedback is reported (Section 2.4, A.2).

The with/without feedback validation only tests immediate refinement on the same question, not accumulated learning across tasks/time; thus the central claim of evaluating continual learning is not fully supported (A.3.5).

The benchmark largely evaluates non-parametric retrieval from feedback logs; only limited SFT on action feedback is tested for parametric updates (A.3.9). It may conflate in-context retrieval of training examples with continual learning.

Baseline comparisons may be unfair: memory systems are run with default parameters and all data attributed to one user identity, long contexts are truncated, and some systems fail on certain datasets (Section 3.1, A.3.2, A.3.8). These choices can disadvantage memory methods and weaken the conclusion that SOTA memory systems are inherently unsatisfactory.

The metric aggregation is not well justified: multiple metrics are merged by LLM-as-judge and then min-max/z-score normalized across heterogeneous datasets; judge reliability and normalization stability are not analyzed (Section 3.2, A.1.2, Tables 7-8).

Data statistics in Table 6 are internally inconsistent (e.g., LiSo total 9364 vs sum ~5473; LiLo total 2100 vs sum 1178; SiSo total 1500 vs sum 750; LoCoMo total 199 vs Table 2/Table 5 1,986), raising concerns about data preparation and reproducibility.
The reproducibility statement is incomplete: it says code/data are open-sourced 'in and' without a URL, and no actual repository link is provided in the manuscript (Section 7).

Presentation needs work: typos and naming inconsistencies ('simluation', 'penalcode', 'Pnalcode'), inconsistent units in Table 14 (it/s vs seconds per sample), and unclear figure/table references (Tables 9 and 14, Figure 3).

There is no dedicated limitations section for the benchmark itself; risks such as simulated feedback bias, overgeneralization from off-policy results, and test-set contamination from public datasets/LLM judges are not adequately discussed (though an ethics statement exists).

On-policy experiments are incomplete because several memory systems are too slow; most conclusions rely on off-policy settings, which are less representative of service-time continual learning (Section 3.2, A.3.6).

strengths: Timely and relevant problem: existing LLM memory benchmarks largely evaluate static, long-context reading comprehension, while this paper targets evaluation of continual learning from user feedback in LLM systems (LLMsys), an under-served area.

Substantial resource: 11 public datasets spanning 3 domains (open/legal/academic), 2 languages, and 4 input/output-length regimes (LiSo, SiLo, LiLo, SiSo), ~20k cases (Table 2), with a clear taxonomy of declarative (semantic/episodic) vs. procedural memory and explicit (verbose/action) vs. implicit feedback, and a useful comparison table positioning prior benchmarks (Table 1).

The user-feedback simulation framework is thoughtfully engineered: a dual-path design (metric-based vs. LLM-as-user), personas/expertise/evaluation criteria, and a probabilistic action model (like/dislike/copy) calibrated to empirical user-behavior statistics (Shuster et al., Chatterji et al.) (Appendix A.2, Tables 3-4).

Useful (if negative) findings: SOTA memory systems (A-Mem, Mem0, MemoryOS) often fail to beat naive RAG, and the efficiency analysis (Figure 3, Table 14) surfaces large memory-operation costs, e.g., MemoryOS memory time far exceeding baselines.

Reproducibility-oriented effort: scripts, user simulators, evaluation pipelines, and simulated feedback logs for open models are claimed to be open-sourced, and there is an ethics statement and reproducibility statement.
Several ablations attempt to isolate the effect of feedback (Tables 11-13) and include on-policy/stepwise experiments (Figs. 4-9), showing some evidence that feedback can help on some datasets.
weaknesses: The central 'continual learning' claim is weakly supported. The headline off-policy setup essentially loads pre-generated training dialogues into memory before testing on a held-out set (retrieval, not continual learning over time). The genuine on-policy continual-learning results are relegated to the appendix for only a few systems, and the curves fluctuate significantly (Figs. 4-6), so the paper does not convincingly demonstrate that MemoryBench measures continual learning.

Validation of the paper's key component - simulated user feedback - is thin. Table 11 shows gains that are frequently marginal or negative (e.g., JuDGE Reasoning Meteor -0.0002, Judge Meteor +0.0008, LexEval-Judge -0.003, LimitGen accuracy 0.0000), and there is no human study establishing that simulated feedback resembles real user feedback or that improvements transfer off the simulator.

Evaluation aggregation is questionable and unstable. Min-max normalization is computed across the tested systems within each dataset, making scores relative and dependent on the baseline set (adding/removing a system changes all scores). Merging heterogeneous metrics via LLM-as-judge and then normalizing across datasets yields aggregate numbers that are hard to interpret, and no variance/significance testing is reported despite small differences (e.g., Embed-S 0.6537 vs. BM25-S 0.6302 in Table 7).

Concrete errors and inconsistencies undermine reproducibility and credibility: Table 6 lists SiSo 'Total' = 1500 while its sample column sums to 750 and the dataset totals sum to 3897; LoCoMo is 1,986 in Table 2/5 but 199 in Table 6; 'SciTechNews' vs. 'JRE-L' naming is inconsistent; Table 9 reports Crime F1 = 0.0000 and Penalcode Index F1 = 0.0000 for every system (broken metrics that are nonetheless fed into the LLM-as-judge integration); Table 14's header says 'iterations per second' while the text and Figure 3 use seconds.

The headline comparison may be unfair. Memory systems are run with default settings and different embedding models (all-MiniLM-L6-v2 for A-Mem/MemoryOS) versus RAG using Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, with different ingestion granularities (per-message vs. per-dialogue) and no tuning. The conclusion that SOTA memory systems are 'unsatisfying' may partly reflect integration/hyperparameter choices rather than fundamental limitations.

The Mem0 'pathological slowdown' is presented as a system property, but no investigation distinguishes a genuine design flaw from an artifact of the integration or the retrieval/consolidation setup; this weakens the efficiency claims.

Limited diagnostic value: the paper is largely descriptive (a repackaged set of existing datasets plus a simulator) and offers little analysis of why memory systems fail or how the benchmark should guide algorithm design; no new method is proposed, and the 'first with all feedback types' claim rests on a self-defined taxonomy.

The LLM-as-user and LLM-as-judge components use models from the same family as the backbone (Qwen), and there is no analysis of potential evaluator bias or of how sensitive conclusions are to the simulator/judge choice.

strengths: Addresses an important gap: existing LLM memory benchmarks largely focus on long-context reading comprehension and static retrieval, while MemoryBench targets procedural memory and continual learning from simulated user feedback.

Comprehensive benchmark construction: collects 11 public datasets across 3 domains, 4 task formats, and 2 languages, with ~20k cases and a useful taxonomy of declarative/procedural memory and explicit/implicit feedback.

The feedback simulation framework is reasonably detailed, combining metric-based scoring for verifiable tasks with an LLM-as-user simulator and probabilistic action modeling for like/dislike/copy behaviors.

Extensive empirical study: reports off-policy, on-policy, and stepwise results; tests multiple RAG and memory-system baselines; includes Qwen3-8B/32B backbones, action-feedback/SFT experiments, and time-consumption analysis.

Provides useful negative findings: SOTA memory systems (A-Mem, Mem0, MemoryOS) do not consistently outperform simple RAG baselines, and several suffer severe latency/scaling issues, which is valuable for guiding future work.
weaknesses: The simulated user feedback is not validated against real human feedback. The with/without-feedback comparisons only show that feedback can improve the current answer, not that the simulated feedback distribution, satisfaction scores, or action probabilities are realistic. Since the benchmark's central claim depends on feedback simulation quality, this is a major validity concern.

The main comparison between advanced memory systems and RAG is confounded by inconsistent embedding models: RAG Embed baselines use Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, while A-Mem and MemoryOS use all-MiniLM-L6-v2. The conclusion that advanced memory systems underperform simple RAG may be partly due to weaker retrieval components rather than memory architecture.

Dataset statistics are inconsistent across the paper. For example, Table 2 reports Locomo with 1,986 cases and DialSim subsets with 1,000 each, while Tables 5/6 report Locomo totals of 1,986 vs. 199 and DialSim totals of 300, and the SiSo totals do not match the individual dataset sizes. This makes the benchmark size, sampling, and splits unclear.

There is a serious metric-reporting inconsistency: Table 9 reports Crime F1 and Penalcode Index F1 as 0.0000 for all systems, despite crime recall/precision being ~0.95/0.97; Table 11 reports nonzero F1 values for JuDGE. This contradiction undermines trust in the reported results and requires explanation/correction.

The test-time protocol is ambiguous. It is unclear what context is given to the LLMsys at test time, whether the test corpus is loaded into memory, and what 'static knowledge relevant to the current question' means. This affects whether the benchmark measures memory utilization, context retrieval, or potential test-time leakage.

The main off-policy experiments use feedback logs generated separately per system, so baselines are not evaluated on a fixed benchmark distribution. This makes cross-system comparison less controlled and raises questions about the fairness of the central comparisons.

Continual learning evaluation is limited: there are no forgetting/backward-transfer metrics, on-policy experiments are only run for fast systems, and parametric continual-learning baselines (SFT/LoRA/RL) are largely relegated to the appendix rather than included in the main benchmark results.

Results are single-run without variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests, and some claims are overstated (e.g., that memory-based LLMsys 'mostly outperformed Vanilla' is not supported across all partitions). The manuscript also lacks an explicit Limitations section and working reproducibility links.

strengths: Addresses an important gap: the lack of benchmarks for evaluating continual learning and memory in LLM systems that involve user feedback over time, as opposed to static long-context reading comprehension.

Provides a comprehensive benchmark integrating 11 existing datasets across multiple domains (open, legal, academic), languages (English, Chinese), and task formats (LiSo, SiLo, LiLo, SiSo), with over 20k cases and a simulation framework (Task Provider, User Simulator, Performance Monitor).

Introduces a well-motivated taxonomy of memory (declarative: semantic/episodic; procedural) and feedback (explicit: verbose/action; implicit), grounded in cognitive science and IR literature, and uses it to categorize existing benchmarks.

Implements a detailed user feedback simulation with both metric-based and LLM-as-user approaches, including probabilistic action models for like/dislike/copy and human annotation to validate feedback quality.

Conducts extensive experiments: off-policy, on-policy, and stepwise settings; multiple backbone LLMs (Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-32B, Mistral3.2-24B); noise analysis for action feedback; time consumption analysis; and case studies.
Open-sources code, data, and simulated feedback logs, with detailed prompts and experimental settings in the appendix, supporting reproducibility.
Includes an ethics statement and discusses limitations of the benchmark and existing systems.
weaknesses: The benchmark does not convincingly evaluate continual learning as defined: the primary off-policy setting pre-generates feedback logs on training data and then uses them as static memory for test queries, which is more akin to retrieval-augmented generation than online continual learning. The on-policy setting is limited and not the main focus.

The user feedback simulation relies on ground-truth evaluation metadata to generate feedback, making the simulator an oracle that provides perfect, task-specific feedback. In real deployment, ground truth is unavailable, so the benchmark may overestimate a system's ability to learn from realistic, noisy feedback.

The human annotation validating feedback quality is weak: only 200 samples, low Fleiss' Kappa (0.093 for naturalness, 0.380 for relevance, 0.273 for overall quality), and win rates of 50–59% are not convincing evidence that simulated feedback is indistinguishable from human feedback. Low Kappa may also indicate poor annotation reliability rather than indistinguishability.

The comparison with memory-based systems (A-Mem, Mem0, MemoryOS) is potentially unfair: the authors use official implementations with default hyperparameters and do not adapt them to the diverse tasks in MemoryBench. Many of these systems were designed for long-context reading comprehension (e.g., LoCoMo) and may require task-specific tuning, which is not performed, biasing results against them.

The evaluation aggregates multiple metrics via LLM-as-judge and then min-max normalization or z-score across datasets. This obscures per-dataset performance and may introduce bias. The main results rely on these aggregated scores, and the high standard deviations shown in Tables 13–14 suggest that many observed differences may not be statistically significant.

The benchmark's novelty is moderate: it combines existing datasets with existing simulation techniques and a taxonomy adapted from prior work. The main finding—that SOTA memory systems underperform naive RAG on procedural memory—is interesting but not deeply analyzed; the paper does not investigate why this occurs or how to improve memory architectures for these tasks.

Many tasks in MemoryBench are single-turn generation tasks (e.g., writing, summarization) where feedback from previous tasks may not transfer meaningfully. The paper does not analyze task similarity or transferability, which is crucial for evaluating procedural memory and continual learning.

The presentation is dense: main text and appendix contain many large tables with small fonts, figures are low-resolution, and some sections are repetitive. The related work comparison in Table 1 is superficial and omits several relevant memory benchmarks (e.g., MemBench, LongMemEval).

The ethics statement is generic and does not address specific risks of the benchmark, such as the potential for simulated feedback to reinforce biases, privacy concerns even with simulated user data, or the environmental cost of running inefficient memory systems.

strengths: The paper assembles a genuinely broad benchmark resource: 11 existing datasets spanning 3 domains (open/legal/academic), 4 task-format categories (LiSo/SiLo/LiLo/SiSo), and 2 languages, with a coherent taxonomy of declarative (semantic/episodic) vs. procedural memory and explicit (verbose/action) vs. implicit feedback. This is a more heterogeneous testbed than prior memory benchmarks such as LoCoMo or DialSim.

The efficiency/time-consumption analysis (Figure 4, Table 19, Figure 11) is a useful and somewhat under-appreciated contribution, documenting that MemoryOS and Mem0 can require tens of seconds to minutes per entry and even pathologically slow down, which is practically relevant for anyone building these systems.

The authors include a human-annotation study (200 cases, 9 annotators) to probe whether simulated feedback is distinguishable from human feedback, and they test multiple settings (off-policy, on-policy, stepwise off-policy, action feedback, noise robustness, and different backbones/simulators), which reflects substantial experimental effort.
A reproducibility statement and open-sourced data/scripts/baselines are provided, and the feedback-log release for off-policy experiments is a reasonable step toward reusable resources.
weaknesses: The feedback simulation is confounded with answer leakage. The LLM-as-user simulator is explicitly given the evaluation context as an "oracle" (golden answer / ground truth) and generates critiques from it; these critiques then become the "procedural memory" fed back to the system. The observed gains (e.g., Table 16) therefore largely reflect the model being handed ground-truth-derived hints rather than demonstrating continual learning from user behavior. This undercuts the paper's central framing.

The headline claim of evaluating "continual learning" is not actually tested. The main experiments are essentially static memory + one-shot feedback injection, and the on-policy results (Figures 5–7) show only small, noisy fluctuations rather than systematic improvement over training steps. Nothing isolates procedural-memory learning from simply adding relevant context.

Several per-dataset evaluations rest on very small test sets. DialSim subsets contain 83–84 sampled cases split 4:1, so the reported accuracies (0.1765, 0.3529, etc.) are computed on ~17 examples, with enormous standard deviations (Tables 13–14). Conclusions drawn at the dataset/domain level are consequently unreliable.

The metric-aggregation pipeline is questionable: native metrics are first merged by an LLM judge into a 1–10 score, then min-max normalized using min/max values tied to one specific baseline's Qwen3-8B off-policy run, then averaged across datasets. This is arbitrary, makes cross-paper comparison meaningless, and can mask or manufacture differences; min-max and z-score tables even give different orderings.

The central empirical finding ("SOTA memory systems do not beat naive RAG") is plausibly an artifact of the setup rather than a clean result. Memory systems are used off-the-shelf with default parameters and retrieval counts, applied to heterogeneous task formats they were not designed for, with contexts truncated to fit. The authors partly concede this (Locomo-specific tuning) but do not disentangle method limitations from benchmark-design choices.

The human-annotation evidence is over-interpreted. Fleiss' Kappa values are very low (0.093 naturalness, 0.273 overall), and win-rates of 50–59% are near chance; the authors read this as showing the simulator is indistinguishable from humans, but low agreement and coin-flip win rates are equally consistent with unreliable annotations and weak discriminability.

Presentation and accuracy issues: Table 9 lists SiSo "Total" as 1500 when the constituent datasets sum to 3897; the Open domain total (10,037) does not match the listed sizes; "3121k" in Table 1 is garbled; capitalization of "MemoryBench" is inconsistent; and phrasing such as "Mem0 has small memory time on tasks with long inputs" is contradictory/unclear.

Limitations and ethics are handled thinly. Table 1 claims support for implicit and action feedback and all memory types, but implicit/action feedback receive only limited appendix experiments, and there is no clear consolidated limitations section addressing the leakage confound or the small-sample reliability problems.

strengths: Proposes MemoryBench, a comprehensive benchmark for memory and continual learning in LLM systems, with a clear taxonomy of declarative (semantic/episodic) and procedural memory plus explicit/implicit feedback. Table 1 credibly positions it as the first to cover all these memory and feedback types.

Collects 11 public datasets spanning open-domain, legal, and academic domains; four task formats (LiSo, SiLo, LiLo, SiSo); two languages; and widely varying input/output lengths (Table 2). This makes the benchmark substantially more heterogeneous than prior long-context reading-comprehension benchmarks.

Introduces a hybrid feedback simulation framework combining metric-based direct evaluation for verifiable tasks and LLM-as-user simulation for subjective tasks, with probabilistic action modeling and released prompt templates (A.2). A human annotation study (A.2.5) provides evidence that simulated feedback is often indistinguishable from human-written feedback.

Runs extensive experiments with naive baselines, RAG variants, and SOTA memory systems (A-Mem, Mem0, MemoryOS) across off-policy, on-policy, stepwise, action-feedback, noisy-feedback, and multi-backbone settings, with detailed per-dataset metrics and efficiency analyses (Tables 10-23, Figures 4-14).

Reproducibility is strong: data, preprocessing scripts, simulators, evaluation pipelines, and baselines are open-sourced; simulated feedback logs are released; the appendix provides dataset descriptions, prompts, hyperparameters, and implementation details.

Provides useful and actionable findings: existing memory systems often fail to consistently beat simple RAG baselines, can be very inefficient (e.g., Mem0 slowdown in Figure 11, MemoryOS memory time in Figure 4), and struggle to utilize procedural feedback, especially in legal and academic domains.

The paper is generally well-structured and transparent about many experimental details, including negative or mixed results (e.g., Vanilla outperforming memory systems on SiLo; limited gains from feedback on some datasets).
weaknesses: The main experiments are off-policy with explicit verbose feedback only; on-policy results are limited to systems fast enough to run (A.3.6). Since continual learning ideally involves online interaction and repeated updates, the central evaluation of continual learning is only partially realized in the main paper.

Experimental evaluation uses sampled subsets of up to 250 instances per dataset rather than the full benchmark, and some per-dataset test sets are very small (e.g., DialSim subsets). No statistical significance tests are reported, despite several comparisons having small margins (e.g., Open-domain differences around 0.006 in Table 10), making some conclusions less robust.

The LLM-as-Judge metric merging can introduce noise or bias and obscures original metrics in the main comparisons; although original metrics appear in the appendix, the aggregated 1-10 scores drive many of the headline conclusions.

The user simulator uses ground-truth/evaluation metadata and a strong LLM (Qwen3-32B) as an oracle-like user. This may generate feedback that is more informative and less noisy than real user feedback. The human annotation evidence is supportive but moderate (win rates around 50-59%, low Fleiss' Kappa), so the claim of high-fidelity simulation is not fully established.

There is no dedicated limitations section for the benchmark itself (e.g., simulator validity, task representativeness, sampling constraints, reliance on LLM-as-Judge). The ethics statement is brief and mostly high-level, though the paper does discuss limitations of existing memory systems.

Some presentation and consistency issues reduce clarity: Table 19 labels time as 'it/s' while Figure 4 describes seconds; Table 1 contains a typo ('3121k'); Figure 3 is a dense radial chart that is difficult to parse compared to the appendix tables.

Baseline fairness is a concern: memory systems are evaluated with default/official settings and without task-specific adaptation, while the paper argues prior studies tailored such systems to Locomo. This supports the general conclusion that out-of-the-box memory systems generalize poorly, but it may understate what optimized memory methods could achieve on MemoryBench.

The claim of being the first comprehensive benchmark is supported relative to the cited works, but it may be somewhat overclaimed given the fast-moving nature of the area and the absence of a broader systematic comparison with all possible recent memory/continual-learning benchmarks.
